heading: A Cree dictionary, a curved church and snow goggles
intro: Indigenous designers and communities solve problems with the same moves this lab teaches: start with people's needs, test, listen to feedback and refine. A Plains Cree dictionary app built in Edmonton, the computer designed buildings of architect Douglas Cardinal and Inuit snow goggles each show a design process at work. Each connection names the people involved, with a source for each claim.

peoples: nêhiyaw (Plains Cree): speakers in Maskwacîs and Moswacîhk
connections.title: itwêwina: a Cree dictionary designed with its users
connections.text: itwêwina is an online Plains Cree dictionary made by the Alberta Language Technology Lab (ALTLab) at the University of Alberta, in collaboration with First Nations University and the Maskwacîs Education Schools Commission. Its spoken word recordings come from speakers in Maskwacîs and Moswacîhk. The team writes that it reconsidered the user interface to "best work on mobile devices" and changed design decisions over time after "feedback from pilot users in the academia and Cree communities." People can search in Cree or English. Settings let each user show Cree words in Roman letters or in syllabics, with plain English, linguistic or Plains Cree labels.

sources.title: Source of the makers, collaborators, recordings and settings (Cree or English search; Roman orthography or syllabics; plain English, linguistic or Plains Cree labels): itwêwina, Plains Cree Dictionary home and settings

Source of the design quotes ("best work on mobile devices"; design decisions changed after "feedback from pilot users in the academia and Cree communities"): Arppe and others, University of Alberta and First Nations University, Towards a morphologically intelligent and user friendly on line dictionary of Plains Cree (Algonquian Conference)
ALTLab: Instructions for providing feedback (beta testers report bugs and suggest features so the dictionary fits "the needs of users")

National Research Council Canada: Intelligent Plains Cree dictionary and word formation project (NRC, ALTLab, Maskwacîs Education Schools Commission and Cree Literacy Network as collaborators; syllabics converter)

connections.title: Douglas Cardinal: people first, computers to help
connections.text: Architect Douglas Cardinal was born in Calgary in 1934. The Canadian Encyclopedia says his father was of Siksika (Blackfoot) and European descent and his mother was of European and Métis ancestry. The Canadian Museum of History says the tent-like roof of his St. Mary's Church in Red Deer "required 82,000 simultaneous equations to design." His firm began using computer-aided design while building that church and became a world pioneer of it. The museum says he looks to "observe how nature has solved its problems" and "places human needs at the heart of the design process." His Alberta buildings include the St. Albert Civic and Cultural Centre and Kainai Middle School.

sources.title: Source of his birth, family heritage (Siksika, European and Métis), computer-aided design (CADD) from St. Mary's Church on, "world pioneer and leader of CADD", and Alberta buildings: The Canadian Encyclopedia, Douglas Joseph Cardinal

Source of the 82,000 equations, "places human needs at the heart of the design process" and "observe how nature has solved its problems": Canadian Museum of History, Architectural Tour, Douglas Cardinal

connections.title: Snow goggles: one problem, many materials
connections.text: Snow goggles solve a clear problem. The Canadian Museum of History says that without them, "people risk snow-blindness, a painful condition likened to a sunburn on the eyes." Iqaluit artist Mathew Nuqingaq, president of the Inuit Art Foundation, says "the slits just [let] you see the horizon and not the snow." The museum says goggles can be made of antler, musk-ox horn, bone, wood or ivory. Carver Ross Kayotak of Igloolik learned from his parents and other carvers. When he had no caribou antler, he carved goggles from bowhead whale rib bone. Nuqingaq now makes them from different materials, including silver.

sources.title: Source of the snow blindness quote, the list of materials and Ross Kayotak's words (taught by his parents and other carvers; bowhead whale rib bone when he had no caribou antler): Canadian Museum of History, Teachers' Zone, Snow Goggles
Source of Mathew Nuqingaq's words on the slits and his silver goggles: CBC Radio, Unreserved, 'They had stories in them': Mathew Nuqingaq explains what drew him to jewelry making
Canada's History: Inuit Snow Goggles, by Amelia Fay (narrow slits limit the light reaching the eyes; snow blindness is "essentially sunburn of the eyes")

try: itwêwina lets each user choose Roman letters or syllabics, and plain English, linguistic or Plains Cree labels. Use Lesson 5 (the self-checkout screen builder) and Lesson 6 (universal design): which universal design principle do these settings use? Then do a quick Investigation 4 style audit: who is helped by each setting, and what would you test next with Cree speakers and learners?

The itwêwina team changed its design after feedback from pilot users in Cree communities and universities. Draw the Lesson 2 design loop and mark where that feedback sent the team back. Why does it matter who the pilot users are? Compare this with testing the boot room prototype in Investigation 1.

Snow goggles meet a need from Lesson 3: protecting your eyes on bright snow and spring ice. Ross Kayotak carved bowhead whale rib bone when he had no caribou antler, and Mathew Nuqingaq uses silver. Douglas Cardinal's team used computers to solve 82,000 equations for one roof. In each case, what stayed the same and what changed? Which Lesson 4 thinking tool helps you separate the important part of a design (the slit, the roof shape) from details you can change?

slide.title: Designing with people in mind
points: Edmonton: itwêwina, a Plains Cree dictionary, changed its design after feedback from Cree community users.
Alberta: architect Douglas Cardinal puts human needs first and used computers to design curved buildings.
Canada: Inuit snow goggles protect eyes from snow; carvers adapt to the materials they have.
slide.notes: Use itwêwina with Lesson 2 (A design process is a loop), Lesson 5 (self-checkout screen builder) and Investigation 4 (Evaluate a user interaction): its settings are a real interface to audit. Use Douglas Cardinal with Lesson 1 (Start with the people, not the gadget) and Lesson 4 (computational thinking). Use snow goggles with Lesson 3 (needs, wants and problems) and Investigation 1 (testing and refining a prototype). Point students to the Ways of knowing section in the lab for sources and discussion prompts.

review_flags: Existing content: the lab and deck have no Indigenous content, sourced or unsourced. The only match is the footer line "Edmonton, Treaty 6 territory", which needs no source. The made up boot room, library kiosk and LRT ticket machine scenarios make no claim about any people.

itwêwina scale: I placed it at Edmonton because ALTLab is at the University of Alberta, but the Cree partners and speakers are in Maskwacîs (and Moswacîhk), so it is also an Alberta story. The project is university led with Cree community collaborators, not Cree led; please confirm you are comfortable with that. No source I fetched says what the Maskwacîs Education Schools Commission did beyond being named a collaborator and providing dictionary entries and recordings, so I did not describe its role. I did not translate "itwêwina" because no page I fetched gave a meaning. Moswacîhk is spelled as on the itwêwina page; I did not identify which community it is. Could ALTLab or MESC suggest a Cree speaker or learner to talk with students about using the app?

Douglas Cardinal: the heritage wording follows The Canadian Encyclopedia exactly (father of Siksika (Blackfoot) and European descent; mother of European and Métis ancestry). Please confirm how he identifies himself; I did not call him Blackfoot or Métis outright. "An Edmonton-based architect" is also on the museum page, so he could fit the Edmonton scale instead. The museum page is an older archived Civilization.ca tour. I did not use a PIN-UP interview (2022) where he describes Elders' visions coming to him in a dream and the 1969 White Paper: important, but it touches spiritual knowledge and politics beyond a design lab. An ArchDaily interview ("A Building Should Be Nurturing and Protect People Within") and a University of Toronto article on St. Mary's Church would not load, so they are not cited.

Snow goggles: the CBC article calls Mathew Nuqingaq president of the Inuit Art Foundation and places his studio in Iqaluit, but does not state that he is Inuk, so I wrote "Iqaluit artist". The CBC page has no date, so "president" may be out of date. Ross Kayotak's community: the museum transcript spells it Iglulik; I used Igloolik. Please confirm both. I did not claim goggles were refined over generations, because no source I fetched says so; the iteration angle is adapting materials, which Kayotak describes himself. I did not use Inuktitut names for goggles because no source I fetched gave one.

Sources rejected: My Modern Met and Ancient Origins snow goggle pieces (not Inuit authored, popular sites); Dartmouth Hood Museum catalogue records (no Inuit voice); a Globe and Mail story on a 3D printed goggle designer (not fetched). City of Edmonton kihciy askiy pages describe Elders guiding the site design (2015 to 2017 consultation), but the site is ceremonial and was already used in the Scientific Observation lab, so I left it out here. I found no well sourced Indigenous universal design or accessibility project to fit CS3.K6 directly; itwêwina's settings are the closest fit.

Science framing: calling itwêwina's settings universal design (flexibility in use) and goggle slits a design solution to a need are my classifications for the lab, not claims in the sources. Please confirm. Would you like to invite a Knowledge Keeper, for example an Inuit carver through an Edmonton Inuit organization, to talk about how tools are made and adapted?

Across the three computer science labs: the itwêwina Plains Cree dictionary (University of Alberta ALTLab with Maskwacîs speakers) also appears in the Programs and Instructions Lab (typing and searching in Cree syllabics) and the Learning Machines Lab (speech synthesis), each time for a different idea. If that feels repetitive for a class doing all three, tell me which lab should keep it and I will find a different connection for the others.
